analysis.title: Two Single Shares, Seven Seats, And A Non-Voting Amazon: Here Is What Anthropic Looks Like On Paper
key_insights: Anthropic's S-1 sets up a control structure separate from economic ownership. A single Class F share held by a Founder LLC (the seven co-founders) carries 50.1% of the vote with no economics, and the 50.1% is fixed so new issuance cannot dilute it.

The seven co-founders hold about 1.69 billion Class A shares combined (roughly 230-245 million each), about 10% of a fully diluted count of roughly 16.9 billion. This is the author's own napkin math, before the founders' pledge to give away 80% of personal equity.
The Class F share is redeemed only if there are fewer than three Continuing Founders for 90 straight days, or if a supermajority of founders agrees to redeem it.

A single Class T share held by the Long-Term Benefit Trust has no economics and no vote on ordinary matters. It elects and removes the four Class T directors, a majority of the seven-seat board, and stays outstanding indefinitely.

Public holders get one vote per share, capped at 49.9% in aggregate. Because the founders' 50.1% votes alongside them on the three non-Trust seats, public holders have no practical say over any board seat. Anthropic will list as a Nasdaq controlled company and use the exemption for its nominating committee.

The post-IPO board has seven seats. Four Class T seats go to Reed Hastings, Vas Narasimhan, Chris Liddell and one vacancy. Three seats go to Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei and Spark Capital's Yasmin Razavi.

Trustees (Neil Shah, Richard Fontaine, Ben Bernanke, Christopher Stubbs, plus one vacancy) are paid $400,000 a year each ($25,000 more for the Chair) by Anthropic. Anthropic sent the Trust $8.4 million in the first nine months of 2026 and made a $450,000 donation to CNAS in August. The Trust is consolidated as a variable interest entity on Anthropic's books.

Class N stock has Class A dividend and liquidation rights but no vote, and converts to Class A when sold to an unaffiliated third party. Holders are mainly strategic compute partners: Amazon and Google (each above 5% after conversions, capped at 12% and 14.99% by their notes), AMD, Broadcom and the Public Benefit Fund.

Google has an option to buy up to $10 billion of Class N stock at the IPO price in a concurrent private placement, plus a $20 billion note facility. AMD committed to buy up to $5 billion of Class N stock as GPUs are delivered starting in 2027. Broadcom's $42 billion note facility converts into Class N at 90% of the 30-day VWAP (85% if revenue targets are missed).

Amazon holds $6.2 billion of non-interest-bearing rollover notes that convert into 1.84 billion Class N shares at fixed prices of $2.09 and $5.05 a share, or the IPO price if lower. At the Series H price of $58.90 per post-split common share, the author estimates they are worth about $108 billion, which is the author's explanation for the $72 billion first-half loss on the income statement.

Vendors hold registration rights over the shares underlying their notes, and the S-1 warns this 'could facilitate sales of large blocks' of Class A stock. Class N converts to Class A on sale, so each strategic stake is potential future supply into the public float.

The Anthropic Public Benefit Fund received 846,840,960 Class N shares (5% of fully diluted). The board approved a framework to issue up to another 2% to the Fund each time the stock rises 50% above the prior milestone, starting at the IPO price.

Two consolidated compute SPVs sign five-year Broadcom master equipment leases for Google TPU hardware with rent of about $161.2 billion excluding interest, guaranteed by Anthropic, PBC. As of June 30 they held $296 million of assets against $328 million of liabilities because most leased capacity is not yet online.

The deal is reportedly valued around $1.5 trillion, the Series H valued Anthropic at $965 billion, and Anthropic expects to match or beat SpaceX's record IPO per Bloomberg. Marketing could start the week of Nov. 9, with Goldman Sachs as lead-left and Morgan Stanley alongside.

The author's conclusion is that public holders get 49.9% of the vote at most and no say over a director, while the founders own about a tenth of the company and the largest outside owners are the vendors sending much of the $637 billion compute invoice.
risk_factors: Governance: the S-1 risk factor says the structure 'may effectively eliminate the ability of holders of our Class A common stock to influence important decisions, including a change in control.'
Public benefit corporation focus on long-term interests may conflict with short-, medium- or long-term financial interests of shareholders.
Supply overhang from vendor registration rights and note conversions of Class N into Class A.
Circularity: hyperscalers invest in AI labs that buy compute from the same hyperscalers, and the Trust, Fund and SPVs concentrate decision-making among the same few people.
Compute commitments of about $637 billion and SPV lease obligations of about $161.2 billion with cross-default provisions.
Valuation of about $1.5 trillion against founder ownership of about 10%.
vol_and_positioning: Strategic holders (Amazon, Google, AMD, Broadcom) have registration rights and note conversions that create pre-arranged supply of Class A shares into the public float after the IPO.
The Public Benefit Fund can receive up to 2% additional shares each time the stock rises 50% above the prior milestone, so dilution arrives when the stock is rising.
cross_bank_references: Jefferies: 'hyperscalers investing in AI labs, which then buy compute from the same hyperscalers, which then book the labs' higher private valuations as profit. Circularity at its finest.'

tension_points.bull_case: Anthropic argues the public benefit structure lets safety and capability win over the next quarter, with directors legally required to weigh more than the stock price. The author notes the structure may work if Claude compounds fast enough that no contested vote is needed.
tension_points.bear_case: Public holders get at most 49.9% of the vote and no practical say over any director. Founders own about 10% of the economics, the Trust owns none, and the largest outside owners are compute vendors with registration rights and a pre-arranged exit.
tension_points.what_invalidates: The first time the growth curve and the compute bill collide, which the author expects would show how little 49.9% of the vote buys.

theme_stances.key_argument: Founders hold about a tenth of the economics but control the vote, and the largest outside owners are vendors with a registered exit.
theme_stances.evidence: public holders will discover just how little 49.9% buys
